name: Name
title: DARK RISING
body: By Aeryn Rudel

name: Name
body: Ancient enemies have returned to the shores of the Iron Kingdoms, and for the first time in centuries, the military might of the kingdom of Khador will find itself challenged by an invading force from beyond the lands of western Immoren. At first, Kapitan Ilari Borisyuk and his forces don’t know what they are seeing—but all too soon, the bloodthirsty invaders known as the Orgoth will make their presence felt and their intentions clear: to crush the nations of the Iron Kingdoms and subjugate its people once again—beginning with Khador. Ilari is not only the first line of defense against the Orgoth; unless he can survive to warn his countrymen, he may well be the only defense. As the Orgoth soldiers, led by the powerful warwitch Sabbreth, called the Eternal Annihilation, pour ashore, Ilari will do what he must for his troops, for his Motherland, and for all of the Iron Kingdoms, even if it means making deadly decisions and impossible sacrifices… Dark Risingis the first book in Privateer’s ongoing monthly Saga series, available through the WARMACHINE app. The first three of six chapters will be available for free; the remaining chapters will continue in monthly installments, along with additional content and features, with a paid WARMACHINE app subscription.

name: Name
body:
After the north gate fell, Ilari fled toward the south end of the city, gathering what troops he could as they retreated from the Orgoth horde. All he’d managed to salvage after his own disastrous battle was the A-2 Bison, his Dire Wolf Nail, and a handful of infantry. Volkova was with him for the first leg of his flight, but after a skirmish with a group of Orgoth reavers, they became separated, and he lost sight of her. With little choice, he pressed on.
The citizens of the port city streamed around Ilari, panicked, horrified. He tried to offer some hope, some sanctuary from the destruction of their lives and homes, but it seemed futile, even to him. He slowed his pace so the mobs of civilians could benefit from his protection as he ushered them toward the south gate, hoping the Orgoth had not yet reached it. It was the only entrance to the city by land, and the Orgoth seemed somewhat reliant on their ships to transport and offload troops.
The soldiers who joined Ilari along his dash through the city seemed desperately grateful for some manner of leadership. Most were Winter Korps infantry, but he also acquired the operator of a battered Man-O-War suppressor and two arkanists. The battle mages had no clue as to the whereabouts of Volkova. Though Ilari looked, and hoped, there was no sign of Lieutenant Roslov and Chief Vislovski, but he couldn’t dwell on that at the moment.

name: Name
body:
The southern gate drew near. It was small and mostly used by merchants and other tradesmen coming into the city overland from Port Vladovar and parts east. It was not defended, its soldiers drawn away to protect other areas besieged by the Orgoth. There was no sign of the enemy, and Ilari breathed a sigh of relief. He called out to the Bison pilot. "Position yourself near the gate. I want your auto cannons covering the road behind us."
He pointed to the great road that led into and through the city. Despite its lack of conventional defenses, the road leading up to the south gate was narrow, pinned in by buildings and stockades designed to service tradesmen. If they were attacked, it would limit the number of enemy troops that could effectively reach them.
He had roughly three units of infantry—not enough to mount any determined resistance but enough to protect the civilians fleeing Skrovenberg for a few crucial moments, if it came to that. He called over the Man-O-War, who had a sergeant’s stripes on his right pauldron. Visions of Nasdovich lying among the countless dead at the north gate rose up in his mind like a grim specter.

name: Name
body:
"Sir," the Man-O-War said and retracted his helmet. He was young, maybe twenty-five, but his ice blue eyes and a ragged scar across his brow spoke of experience and competence.
"What’s your name?" Ilari asked.
"Nowak, sir. Yuri Nowak."
"Sergeant Nowak, take two detachments of the infantry and provide an escort as best you can to any civilians fleeing the city. Head directly south and stay away from the Lothpool." The Orgoth would likely send their ships up the deep, wide river. "If I do not catch up with you, tell whoever commands the defenses of Port Vladovar what has happened here, what you’ve seen. Do you understand?"
"Perfectly, sir."
"Good man. Go."
Sergeant Nowak chose his troops—mostly riflemen—and left Ilari the sole machine gunner and two of the rocketeers. He then organized frightened civilians into something resembling an orderly exodus and disappeared through gate after the last of Skrovenberg’s citizens made it through.
Ilari took up a position on the opposite side of the gate to the Bison. He faced Nail in the same direction as the Bison’s auto cannons. The Dire Wolf’s bombard was running low on ammunition, but a few well-placed blasts might slow down the advancing enemy. The ten soldiers he had with him were haggard, wounded, or shell-shocked, all of them survivors of battles lost. A few of them glanced back to where Sergeant Nowak had gone, obviously wishing they had gone with him.

name: Name
body:
They waited. Minutes passed in slow agony. Ilari could see flames blooming within the city to the north; he could hear the howls of the enemy. Those screeching calls grew louder, and the road to the south gate soon became clogged with armored bodies.
The Orgoth had found them.
It seemed every time Ilari thought he’d become accustomed to the Orgoth terror, something new and ghastly appeared to prove him wrong. A group of armored wraith-like figures drifted ahead of two dozen oversized ogrun-like creatures. The brutes were armed with a battle-axe in each oversized fist while the wraiths’ or witches’ armor was the typical style he’d seen with all the Orgoth—spiked and shaped to resemble beasts, insects, or some horrible amalgamation of the two. These figures had long braided hair and each clutched a two-handed blade. At first glance, they seemed to be warriors, but then he realized they were something far worse.
One of the witches shouted in a barking, alien tongue, and the axe-bearing brutes charged.

name: Name
body: The Khadoran infantry fired their rifles, then the Bison’s auto cannons opened up, reducing the first line of the enemy to bloody rags. As one, each of the witches became shrouded in a cloak of misty darkness, and they advanced like floating motes of void. Ilari raised his rifle and fired at one, but his shot went wide—there was simply nothing to aim at. Spell runes appeared around the witches’ darkened shapes. Gouts of greenish flame erupted from their presence, and the flames caught a handful of the Winter Korps infantry. They did not burn. Instead, the flesh fell away from their bones in a liquid tide. They weren’t even given the merciful time to scream. More Orgoth troops arrived, but the axers had fallen among the few remaining soldiers. Ilari wanted to send Nail charging in, to gun down as many of these new foes as possible, but Volkova’s words would not let him. You cannot die here. "Pull back through the gates," he shouted to the Bison driver and then relayed the same order to the half-dozen infantry nearest him.

name: Name
body:
The driver needed no further encouragement, and the Bison rumbled away. Ilari followed with Nail by his side. There were still Winter Korps soldiers battling the enemy, holding them at bay in front of the gates.
On the road outside, Ilari took in a deep breath and gave the order that would haunt him for the rest of his life. "Fire at the gate. Bring it down!"
The Bison driver took no issue with the order—his auto cannons ripped into the stone wall above and around the gates. Ilari added Nail’s bombard, and in moments, the gate collapsed, huge blocks of stone crashing down in an avalanche of dust and mortar. Screams of pain still reached Ilari through the makeshift barricade.
He turned away from the dying Skrovenberg and gave the order to move south. The first Khadoran city had fallen to the Orgoth.
Two miles outside the city, Ilari caught up to Sergeant Yuri Nowak and the soldiers he’d sent with the Man-O-War. The sergeant seemed to be waiting for him, yet the civilians Ilari had ordered Nowak to protect were gone.

name: Name
body:
As he approached, Ilari demanded, "Where are the people I sent with you?"
"Sir, I sent them on," Nowak said. "They were slowing us, and I believe that makes all of us more vulnerable."
Ilari agreed with the assessment, but the sergeant couldn’t just leave a hundred men, women, and children undefended. "Explain yourself."
"Yes, sir," Nowak said. He sounded confident—sure of himself but not haughty. "The Orgoth seem to be focusing their attacks on more strategic targets."
"From what we’ve seen, yes."
"So, they’re unlikely to spend much if any resources navigating rough terrain after a few hundred civilians," Nowak continued. "Blackroot Forest is only a couple of miles from here. I sent the civilians there."
It made sense. The Orgoth would be looking for bigger prizes, like those to be found in Port Vladovar. Ilari sighed. "All right. Good thinking, sergeant. Those people may survive because of you."
"Thank you, sir," Nowak said. He suddenly looked so young, beaming beneath the praise.
They still had issues to attend to, primarily the fuel reserves of the Bison and Ilari’s Dire Wolf. He approached the smoke-spewing vehicle. The driver looked down at him, a gaunt-faced man with small eyes and wispy brown hair.

name: Name
body:
"What’s your name, Sergeant?" Ilari called up.
"Radovich, sir," the man said.
"Sergeant Radovich, we’re going to abandon the Bison, and I want you to—"
"Abandon it?" Radovich said, scoffing. "You can’t be serious."
Ilari cocked his head in disbelief. Here was another element of command new to him: insubordination. "I am quite serious, sergeant. You’re going to transfer the coal in this machine to Nail, my Dire Wolf, and you’re going to do it immediately. You will also address me as sir from this point forward."
"Sir, I think the Bison will provide us more firepower if we run into the enemy," Radovich said, his tone more measured.
"And I think, as a warcaster, that a warjack possesses all the firepower we need without alerting the entire countryside to our presence. I also think I am a kapitan and you are a sergeant and that you will follow my order without question or by Thamar’s black breath I’ll have you in chains." Ilari hadn’t meant to be that harsh, and he was just as rattled as any of the soldiers around him, but he couldn’t let them see that. His anger had the desired effect, though.

name: Name
body:
Radovich’s face was ashen. "My apologies, sir."
"Sergeant Nowak," Ilari called out, ignoring Radovich for now, "please assist Sergeant Radovich. There should be enough coal for your suppressor armor as well."
Once they had Nail refueled, he glanced back toward Skrovenberg. There, greasy plumes of black smoke rose into the sky, and he thought he could hear what might be screams. He told himself it was just the wind and led his tattered forces south.
He ordered a double-time march; they needed to make up time and to reach Port Vladovar quickly. They soon reached the Great Road that ran between the Kulvorn Hills and the Blackroot Forest. It was wide and even, and though he loathed the thought of traveling on something so obvious a target, it would get them to Point Vladovar faster, and there had been no sign of pursuit so far.
They marched through what remained of the day and then through the dawning night. The temperature dropped, and their pluming breath mingled with black smoke from Nail’s furnace. Ilari had sent an advance scout ahead to see what lay farther up the road. The woman came back at a trot from the north. She was gray-haired, likely pushing fifty, and brought decades of valuable experience to them—Ilari knew she could be counted on. Indeed, Korporal Ayakaz Petrova was a Kossite, and she had once served Khador as a woodland scout. "I saw soldiers two miles up. Near the edge of the woods."

name: Name
body: "Ours or the enemy?" Ilari asked. "Looks like ours by the smoke and the firelight. ’Jack furnaces likely." "Numbers?" "I would estimate as many troops as we have, sir," Petrova said. "Well done." He ordered an advance with Nowak and himself in the lead. While he had every confidence in Petrova’s intel, he couldn’t afford to take any chances. So, he placed Nail up front. The warjack would draw fire, and his plow shield would protect them from small arms, giving Ilari enough time to use his magelock and spells if necessary. He held back the infantry about a hundred yards, hidden by a slight bend in the road. If an enemy attacked, they could return fire with some element of surprise. As he neared the spot Korporal Petrova had described, he could see a telltale plume of smoke, blacker than the night sky, and he relaxed. He’d seen nothing like that among the Orgoth forces, so he took a chance. "Sons and daughters of the Motherland!" he shouted. "We serve in the empress’ name!" came the correct reply.

name: Name
body:
Half a dozen shapes separated from the trees, one of them a warjack, its furnace unmistakable in the dark. The shapes approached, and one of them lit a flare—a blow torch, in truth.
"By Thamar’s bloody teeth, sir, it is damned good to see you again," Chief Vislovski said.
Ilari reached out and took the mechanik’s hand, gripping it tightly. "You as well, Chief. Who else is with you?"
"We made it out with about fifty infantry." Vislovski gestured to the trees behind him. "Lieutenant Roslov is there with them."
"Roslov is alive?" Ilari said, unable to believe his good fortune. There had been precious little of that lately.
"The lieutenant dragged me and everyone she could away from that gate when it fell," Vislovski said. "Fights like a demon, that one, and leads like a bloody kommandant."
"If we survive this, I’ll be the first to put her up for a promotion."
"Nasdovich?" Vislovski asked softly.
Ilari shook he head. "I’m here only because of her."
"A shame," Vislovski said. "The Motherland needs fearless soldiers like her now more than ever."

name: Name
body:
"While I draw breath, she will not have died in vain."
"I believe it, sir. Orders?"
"We join up and make for Port Vladovar."

name: Name
body:
Lieutenant Roslov had salvaged more than just standard infantry; somewhere along her flight through the city, she’d also found a single unit of the heavily armed shock trooper gunners. Their massive scatterguns, tearing chain blades, and thick armor made them the equivalent of twice their number in standard troops.
Ilari took control of the warjack Vislovski had been leading. It was armed with an ice hammer and a heavy chain gun attached to its left fist. The chain gun reminded Ilari of Nasdovich, and when he made contact with the new Dire Wolf, her name came to him with a sad smile. "Koshka."
Ilari was fortunate that Vislovski hadn’t just escaped with a Dire Wolf. He’d also had the presence of mind to nab two ’jack carts, each pulled by a pair of draft horses. Nail and Koshka’s fuel reserves had been supplemented when they passed through civilized areas outside Cygnar, and they’d been able to procure enough coal to keep them going. Those opportunities were at and end, however, and their current reserves would not let them get all the way to Port Vladovar, some sixty miles away. They powered down the two warjacks and loaded them on the carts. It would force them to travel on the road, but they’d have the extra firepower if they needed it.

name: Name
body: They were on the Great Road for two straight days with no sign of the enemy and making good time, twenty-five miles per day. On the eve of the third day, just as the sun was sinking below the horizon, Roslov joined Ilari at the head of their procession, a worried look on her face. "We haven’t seen any of the enemy, sir. Don’t you find that odd?" Ilari had been thinking about the very same thing. "Maybe not. The distance between Port Vladovar and Skrovenberg is too great for an army that undisciplined. You’ve seen them fight. They’re little more than dogs let off their leashes. A long march inland, and they’d lose control of their army. I think they’re going to sail down the coast, make for the Bay of Kulvorn, and attack Vladovar from there." "You don’t see them taking any forces overland like they did in the Vescheneg Headlands?" Roslov said. Ilari didn’t miss the edge to her question. "I gather you do?" "I’m looking for patterns, sir. They sent troops after us when we left Brone’s Point, likely to keep us from warning Skrovenberg," she said. "That was purposeful. The act of someone planning, thinking ahead. I think we should prepare for them to do the same if they think anyone will reach Vladovar first."

name: Name
body:
"You may be right, but we’re as prepared as we can be."
"Yes, sir," Roslov said, but that worried look remained.
It grew darker as they neared Port Vladovar. The clouds covered the moon, and the stretch of rocky ground between the road and the east side of the city forced Ilari to power up the warjacks. Their furnaces glowed with enough light to act as beacons for the soldiers to follow, but they’d also be easy to spot if there were any Orgoth waiting to ambush them.
Three miles from the east gate of Port Vladovar, the darkness was almost impenetrable. A deep unease crept over Ilari as they advanced, almost blind, the furnaces of Koshka and Nail providing only enough illumination to keep them from stumbling over the uneven ground.
Finally, with the gates in sight, Ilari took a chance. He chambered a runeshot in his magelock, pointed his weapon at the sky, and fired. Three hundred feet in the air, the round burst into a cluster of brilliant motes that drifted slowly earthward, illuminating everything for quite a distance. What the light revealed seized Ilari’s guts with terror.

name: Name
body:
The Orgoth had crept to within a hundred yards of their position. The flare round showed a force of some two hundred reavers. Leading them was a nightmarish figure, a woman clad in savage armor, a fan of blades projecting from her back, and a long, curved sword in each hand. The smoldering glow from her armor and the two grotesque warjacks by her side could mean only one thing: Ilari and Volkova had surmised in Skrovenberg that if the Orgoth had warjacks, they must have warcasters. It was no longer conjecture. It was an awful truth.
"Firing line! Firing line!" Ilari shouted as the light faded to let the darkness swallow them again. He could still see the ember-like flicker from the enemy warjacks as they moved, but the Winter Korps infantry opened up firing blindly at the enemy. The pair of rocketeers fared better; the fiery dagger of ignition provided a flash of illumination and then another as the rockets struck and exploded among the charging Orgoth.
Ilari used the rockets’ brief illumination to search for the enemy warcaster again. When he found her, he fired at her with his magelock. The shot was true, but it should have punched a hole through armor and anything behind it. Instead, a gauzy dome of red light flickered into existence for a brief moment, long enough to deflect the bullet, and then darkness fell again, leaving Ilari with the knowledge that not only did the Orgoth possess warcasters, but their technology was at least as advanced as his own.

name: Name
body:
Now came the barking fire of the Orgoth weapons as they discharged in a strobing ripple of red light. Projectiles bounced off Ilari’s power field or off the hulls of Koshka and Nail. He could hear the Orgoth rushing in their direction; they’d be in melee range soon. He fired Nail’s bombard, providing a momentary burst of light when the explosive shell landed. He aimed Koshka’s chain gun at the same spot, ripping into the enemy with a storm of bullets.
Ilari chambered another round, fired the flare into the sky, and then the Orgoth fell on them. He saw their warcaster and her warjacks charging in his direction, and he fired two shots at her. One missed and the other sent her reeling back with a loud oath in a clipped guttural tongue.
The Orgoth warjacks reached Ilari first, but Nail and Koshka intercepted them. The Dire Wolfs’ furnaces and the crimson radiance of the enemy warjacks’ fiery cores provided an eerie sheen to their combat. Koshka’s ice hammer flashed blue as it impacted the hull of an Orgoth ’jack armed with a spiked mace and shield. The second enemy warjack struck sparks from Nail’s plow-shield with a long-bladed polearm, then followed this by punching a fist-mounted spike over the Dire Wolf’s shield and into his hull. Ilari registered the damage, but at least it wasn’t severe.

name: Name
body:
He prepared to push arcane power into his warjacks’ strikes when his power field blazed with blue light, an azure flash in the darkness, as a heavy blade slashed against it. The Orgoth warcaster came at him in a whirling flurry of blades, steel glinting like blood in the pulsing glow of her armor. Ilari staggered back, blocking a strike with his rifle and hammering its butt into the Orgoth’s chest, pushing her away. In that brief respite, he chambered a round and fired. The armor-piercing runeshot punched through the bladed warcaster’s power field. It sapped the energy from the round, though, which impacted harmlessly against her armor.
She didn’t come at him again. Instead, she uttered a harsh string of syllables and a ring of spell runes formed around her. She pointed a finger at Ilari. The runes vanished, and blasphemous arcane power washed over him. The strength went out of his limbs; his rifle sagged in his grip. The Orgoth warcaster rushed in, her blades whirling. Ilari managed to draw his sword—its weight was ponderous and clumsy—and parry one attack, but the second scored his left arm, and a line of agony blazed across his limb. He dropped his rifle and backpedaled, reaching out to his warjacks to aid him. Both were locked in combat with the Orgoth ’jacks, and he felt Nail wanting to pull away, to come to Ilari’s rescue, but he knew the ’jack would be destroyed if he did.

name: Name
body:
The Orgoth warcaster did not follow up with her weapons; instead, spell runes circled her body again, and her lips beneath her half-helm twisted in a savage approximation of a smile. The magic coalesced, and a bolt of black energy struck Ilari squarely, burning his flesh and sucking the breath from his lungs. Desperate, he cast a spell of his own, dropping a cloud of impenetrable darkness over himself. It blinded him completely, but it would limit his foe’s sight as well.
The lingering weakness in his limbs began to fade. He felt naked without his rifle; he already knew that he was no match for the Orgoth warcaster in melee. He concentrated and viewed the world through Koshka’s eyes. The Dire Wolf had its opponent reeling, nearly destroyed, and their battle had drifted close to his own. Ilari concentrated and summoned his most powerful magic. At the Druzhina, he’d been taught that each warcaster was possessed of a unique arcane skill—one derived from their experience, personality, the very makeup of who they were. Once unlocked, it was a powerful tactical asset. He would have to time it perfectly, or he would die.

name: Name
body:
"Come and face Sabbreth, worm," the Orgoth warcaster hissed from somewhere. She spoke something akin to old Caspian, close enough that Ilari could understand her. "I am your annihilation. Face the inevitable. You cannot win."
Ilari’s magical darkness faded, and he stood exposed, the fire from his warcaster armor marking his position. "I’m here."
The warcaster who had called herself Sabbreth pivoted and sprinted toward him, her twin blades spinning in a deadly geometric whirl. Ilari unleashed his magic—in his head he heard the piercing howl of a wolf, an animal that depended on its pack, cooperating to take down a creature stronger than himself.

name: Name
body:
Through his link with Koshka, he felt the Dire Wolf reduce the Orgoth warjack to wreckage, and then Ilari’s magic took hold, granting the Dire Wolf preternatural speed. Sabbreth was nearly on top of Ilari when Koshka came thundering out of the dark, her ice hammer a bolt of blue lightning. The Orgoth warcaster attempted to duck the blow, but Ilari flooded Koshka’s strike with the last of his magic, guiding it unerringly. The hammer struck Sabbreth with a rending sound of steel on steel, sending her hurling backward, her breastplate crumpled, her blades flying from her hands.
Now Ilari charged, taking his sword in both hands as Sabbreth attempted to rise to her feet. He lunged leading with his blade and plunged it deep into the Orgoth warcaster’s abdomen. She let out a pained scream and fell back. He went with her, landing on top, his hand still around the weapon. He ripped it out. Blood sprayed his face. He was about to drive the blade home again, when Sabbreth spoke, and her voice caused him to falter.

name: Name
body: "If you kill me, it means nothing. I will come again, and everything you know and love will still fall," she whispered and tried reaching for one of her blades. Ilari put his sword under her throat, and she stopped. Apparently she was not yet ready to die. It dawned on him then that if he could take this Sabbreth captive, they could learn about much about the Orgoth’s purpose. He glanced around the battlefield, seeing Vislovski’s torch burning brightly amidst a throng of battling Winter Korps and Orgoth reavers. He felt Nail reduce the warjack he’d been battling into scrap, and Ilari called the Dire Wolf to his side. "You’ll find the Khadoran people are not so easy to destroy," he said, pushing his blade into the pale skin beneath Sabbreth’s helm until it drew a bead of blood. He ached to end her, to remove this monstrous abomination from the face of Caen. Wisdom held him in check. She chuckled, low and awful. "Fool. Your dark prince has fallen. The prophecy of Dagholoth is nigh."

name: Name
body: Nail arrived and stood over them, his furnace lighting Sabbreth’s face with a bloody hue. "What prophecy?" Ilari snarled. "Why are you here?" Sabbreth laughed again. "To stain the seas with blood." She placed her hand around Ilari’s blade, blood oozing between her fingers, and drew herself closer to him. "Nothing will save your souls. Nothing." At that moment, overcome with sick horror, Ilari raised his sword to end Sabbreth. It didn’t matter; she said as much. So be it. But the battle had flowed in their direction, and Nail moved to intercept the enemy. One, a hulking reaver with sword and shield, skirted around the Dire Wolf and came barreling at Ilari. He jerked his sword up to meet the new threat, but the Orgoth warrior did not swing his own weapon. He simply threw himself at Ilari and onto his blade, knocking him away from Sabbreth and pinning Ilari beneath the warrior’s hulking weight. More Orgoth troops evaded Nail’s plow-shield, and ran toward Sabbreth, grabbed her up. Koshka killed two of them with her ice hammer, but the Orgoth succeeded in bearing their leader away.

name: Name
body: Ilari pushed the dead Orgoth warrior off him and cast about for his rifle. It was still dark, but some god took mercy on him as he nearly tripped over the bulky weapon. He reached for it, his wounded arm still throbbing, managed to shoulder the magelock and fired another flare rune shot. It lit up a desperate scene. Khadoran soldiers lay dead and butchered among enemy dead, and what remained of his forces was about to be overwhelmed. Ilari took a deep breath and set his rifle down. He was out of runeshots, and he drew his sword again as Orgoth warriors came at him in a howling horde. Nail and Koshka swept many of them aside with ice hammer and plow-shield, but their targets were not the warjacks. The Orgoth were coming for him this time. Ilari braced for death. But no Orgoth reached him. The staccato burst of an auto cannon sounded, and the Orgoth closest to him came apart in eruptions of red mist. He glanced to the west, to Port Vladovar, and heard the thunder of hooves, saw hundreds of flickering lights. Not torches but the blasting pikes of a hundred shock trooper pikemen.

name: Name
body: They slammed into the Orgoth ranks, detonating in a ripple of destruction, reducing any Orgoth on the other end of a pike to gory chunks. They took down one of the Orgoth warjacks in the same way, cracking its hulls and blowing it apart. Then came the light infantry, firing their rifles before closing with axe and sword. Ilari ordered Nail and Koshka into the battle, but the Dire Wolfs were not needed. For the first time, the Orgoth retreated. They fled to the north harried by rifle and auto cannon fire. They were not followed, however, could not be chased. Ilari collapsed to the ground, exhausted, bleeding, and emotionally drained. Two figures separated from the crowd of soldiers. One, he recognized. Magziev Volkova’s armor was bent and burned in places, but she’d somehow survived the flight from Skrovenberg and made it to Port Vladovar on her own. If anyone could, it would be her, Ilari thought. The second figure seemed to walk out of the past from a time before Khador had been fractured and diminished in the Claiming. Assault Kommander Oleg Strakhov stood tall and straight, though his years were visible on his face in a crisscross pattern of scars, an eyepatch over his right eye, and the overall weathered appearance of a man who had spent the majority of his life in armed conflict. His armor was archaic by modern standards, a lighter warcaster kit with a pair of stacks. He gripped a short-barreled carbine with a drum magazine, and a pair of long trench knives was sheathed on each leg.

name: Name
body:
Ilari staggered to his feet and leaned on his rifle like a crutch, an action that would have horrified old Toskar.
"Kommander Strakhov," he said. "I thought . . ."
"That I was dead," Strakhov said with the ghost of a smile. His visible eye grew distant, haunted. "You’re not alone. But maybe I should be."
He came back to himself instantly, the iron discipline for which he was legendary reasserting itself. "The Magziev has told me much about you, Kapitan Borisyuk. You made it all the way from Ice Watch?"
"I did, sir," Ilari said. "I had to. I was the first to see the Orgoth, so I had to warn as many as possible."
"Impressive," the old warcaster said, and that single word filled with Ilari with such pride he almost forgot the horror he’d just experienced.
"I encountered one of their warcasters. A woman called Sabbreth," Ilari said, knowing he must pass on what he’d learned. "We fought. I overcame her, had her at my mercy. But I did not strike the death blow."
"Why not?" Volkova asked, speaking for the first time.

name: Name
body:
"I thought to take her captive," Ilari said. "Then she spoke of . . . strange things." Now that the battle had ended, Sabbreth’s words rose in his mind like corpses floating on the surface of still water.
"What did she say?" Strakhov said.
"She spoke of a dark prince and a prophecy by someone called Dagholoth."
Volkova gasped—it was more emotion than Ilari had ever seen from her before.
"You know this name?" Strakhov asked.
"All Greylords know Dagholoth," she whispered. "He was a great oracle, a doomsayer. We were forbidden from plundering his tomb in the Wyrmwalls, as we did with all Orgoth cairns."
"What of this dark prince?" Ilari asked. The appellation sounded familiar, but he couldn’t quite place it.
Strakhov drew in a deep breath. "The only Dark Prince I know of is Great Prince Vladimir Tzepesci. He was a powerful warrior and sorcerer."
Strakhov was silent for a moment, and a look came over his face Ilari had seen many times. War was horror, and soldiers who had seen too much of it lost a piece of themselves to the darkness. "He fell at Henge Hold."

name: Name
body:
"He was the empress’ consort," Volkova added. "They had a son."
"I don’t understand," Ilari said. "How would the Orgoth who haven’t seen these shores in centuries know anything about Vladimir Tzepesci?"
"Dagholoth was reputed to be a powerful oracle," Volkova said definitively, as if that were enough of an answer. It wasn’t, but Ilari had no idea what else to ask.
He shook this all off. "I say we put no stock in this Sabbreth’s words. I was about to kill her. She was desperate to stay my blade and would have said anything to do so. Including an old ghost story."
"I must go to Korsk," Strakhov said, abruptly changing the subject. "I will lead what remains of Port Vladovar’s forces and civilians there."
Ilari asked, "What of their warships?" He had thought the fleet at the port city might stymie the Orgoth advance to some degree.
The kommander took a deep breath. "Destroyed at sea by the Orgoth armada. I was sent to bolster the city’s defenses, but it is lost and will fall within days."
"My officers and I will go with you," Ilari said. He refused to entertain the idea that Roslov and Vislovski had not survived. It was too cruel.

name: Name
body: Strakhov shook his head. "No, you will go to the Wyrmwalls." He glanced at Volkova. "You as well." Ilari was taken aback. "Sir, you can’t believe that Sabbreth spoke truth. I would be of more use—" "I will decide where you will be of more use," Strakhov said, rubbing at the gray stubble on his chin. "Kapitan Borisyuk, this is an enemy we know almost nothing about, an enemy no one has seen in thousands of years. Anything we learn about them may help us. Perhaps this Sabbreth was lying or perhaps there was some truth in her words. Either way, we must know." A deep chill ran through Ilari’s body and he looked to the south where the great chain of mountains lay within the borders of Cygnar. It was a thousand-mile trek at least. "More often than not, intel wins wars, Kapitan," Strakhov continued. "Learn an enemy’s purpose, learn their weakness, and then exploit both." "Yes, sir," Ilari said flatly. He’d said his piece and would not argue further. It did not mean he agreed. "Good. Return to Korsk when you know more," Strakhov said. "Take what supplies and troops you need."

name: Name
body:
Ilari looked over at Volkova, and he saw something he didn’t expect. The magziev was afraid.
Lieutenant Roslov’s right arm was in a sling, and a heavy bandage on her face covered a deep cut from an Orgoth blade. Vislovski had emerged from the battle unscathed, so he fussed over Koshka and Nail as Ilari addressed his officers. Volkova had joined the small group as well and still wore her armor, battered as it was.
Ilari began. "You have been through the unthinkable with me. From Ice Watch to the gates of Port Vladovar." He glanced back at the city that would soon fall. They were safe for the moment, surrounded by Strakhov’s troops. "And I must ask yet more of you."
"Ask it, sir," Roslov said.
"Volkova and I must go to the Wyrmwall Mountains. There we must uncover an ancient Orgoth tomb."
Vislovski moved to stand in front of Koshka. "Why not go to Korsk with Kommander Strakhov, sir? The city will need defenders."
Ilari struggled to hide his doubt. He still did not agree with Kommander Strakhov. "Assault Kommander Strakhov believes the tomb may hold vital intelligence on the Orgoth. Volkova and I have been ordered to retrieve it.

name: Name
body: "Orgoth tombs hold many secrets," Volkova said. "The warlord entombed there was known to be an oracle of great power." Ilari gave Volkova a long, appraising look. She was a believer, and why shouldn’t she be? Her former order had more experience with the Orgoth than anyone in Immoren. If she believed, then perhaps there was something to Sabbreth’s dire predictions. But he still had the feeling this was an empty chase that would keep him from chasing the real enemy. "That’s all we can tell you for the moment," Ilari said. "But I can think of no finer soldiers to have at my back as we make this trek. I will not order you to come with me. It must be your decision." They were all silent for a moment, then Roslov stepped forward. "I doubted your command, sir. I won’t lie about that." Ilari nodded. How could she not? He had doubted it himself. "But I now believe you to be one of the finest officers in the Winter Korps," Roslov continued. "You pushed on when lesser soldiers would have faltered. Led us through horror and pain without concern for yourself." She paused and drew herself up straight. "I would be honored to follow you once more."

name: Name
body:
Vislovski joined Roslov, towering over the lieutenant. "I’m not as gifted with words as the lieutenant is, but she speaks true. I’m with you.’ He chuckled. "You’ll need someone to keep your warjacks in fighting shape."
That these two exemplary soldiers would again risk their lives to fight beside him nearly overwhelmed Ilari with emotion: pride and the intense camaraderie that can only be earned on the battlefield . . . and by a good commander.
"You honor me," he said as he looked to the south, where the tomb of Dagholoth waited in the forbidding Wyrmwalls. All the pride and hope he had just felt moments before disappeared before a sudden and inevitable cold wind of dread.

name: Name
body:
The last thing Sabbreth saw before she lost consciousness was Drashak flinging himself at Borisyuk and knocking the Immorese battle wizard away before he could land the killing blow to her. After that, the world grayed, then blackened, and she spun into oblivion.
She felt the presence of her Fellgoeth masters, their whispering voices slithering into her mind and filling it with images, messages, and portents from the lightless abyssal halls. They showed her possible futures, some of which she herself had set in motion.
The images became overwhelming, and Sabbreth fought her way back to consciousness. When she opened her eyes, she had no concept of how long she had been in the dark. She lay on her back, staring up at a dawn sky painted grim with ash and smoke. The wounds she’d sustained remained, and they throbbed with the searing ache of knitting flesh. No doubt, one of the warwitches had expended precious soul energy to heal Sabbreth’s wounds. A debt she would have to account for later.

name: Name
body:
She sat up with a wince and saw she was still among her horde, now encamped beyond the walls of Port Vladovar. The eastern gate and its causeway that spanned the river had been sundered, blown apart by some great force. Horruskh had entered the city there. The thought of her rival reaping the bounty of the fallen city while she lay insensate from her wounds sent both panic and rage buzzing through her body.
Sabbreth’s armor had been shut down, so she fired up its blaze furnace and stood. The movement sent shards of agony through her body, and she nearly went to her knees. Then she saw dozens of her reavers and other soldiers watching her, searching for yet more weakness beyond what she’d already shown. Her hands fell to the hilts of her swords, and her spectators found other business to occupy their attention.
Pushing her way through the horde toward the city, Sabbreth reached out to the pair of Jackals that had accompanied her since the Orgoth had made landfall. She could no longer sense them, which might mean they were too far away or, worse, might mean Horruskh had taken them for himself.

name: Name
body:
As she drew near the river, she saw hundreds of Immorese prisoners herded into ragged lines. They were chained and most bore wounds of some kind. Fearful wails and pleas for mercy erupted from the crowd. They were not silenced. Their terrified clangor was a paean of Orgoth victory.
Among the soldiers and spoils of war loomed a familiar and terrible figure. Horruskh, the Thousand Wraths was a giant of steel and blood. He stood closer to eight feet than seven, and his elaborate armor seemed to be made from snarling demonic faces. His blaze furnace spread from his back like great iron wings, and he gripped the hilt of his enormous abyssal blade, its point digging into the Immorese earth, as if he were intent on laying claim to every piece of this land. He pointed and shouted at nearby reavers, directing them to move prisoners onto ships waiting in the river or to lead them toward groups of warwitches for sacrifice.
As Sabbreth approached, Horruskh removed his helm. The face beneath was a visage shaped and molded by pain and violence. One side of Horruskh’s mouth was half-melted by acid burns. It pulled that side of his lips down in a perpetual frown. His nose has been broken so many times it had lost its original shape, and all that remained was a smashed lump of flesh below his eyes. If his face were the legacy of pain, Horruskh’s eyes were the promise. They were large, almost goggling, but a shade of brown so dark, they appeared black in the fitful light of the dawn. They had witnessed horrors uncountable, and they were a barren place where no warmth or mercy could gain purchase.

name: Name
body: "Sabbreth," Horruskh said, his mangled lips turning up in a grotesque half-smile. His voice was a hoarse whisper, thanks to another scar across his throat. "I hope you have recovered from your . . . defeat." The word was a knife to Sabbreth’s guts, one she wanted to pull from her flesh and bury in Horruskh’s face. "I have not failed," she said and pointed at the ruined city beyond the river. "I secured many souls, crushed many enemies—" "All but one," Horruskh cut her off and chuckled. "You were saved, Sabbreth. Spared death by a lowly reaver captain. How undignified." Sabbreth realized Drashak had traded his life for hers. Fool, she thought. She felt no gratitude for the reaver, for she would never risk so much for someone of so little consequence. "I saw one of the enemy battle wizards killing many of your troops," Sabbreth said, jabbing at Horruskh with one of his failures. "Did you capture him?" The muscles in Horruskh’s jaws jumped as he ground his teeth together. "He escaped."

name: Name
body:
"So, you, too, let a great offering slip through your fingers?"
Horruskh stared at Sabbreth in silence, then said, "Kishtaar has made landfall and marches north toward a city called Ohk."
Sabbreth ignored Horruskh’s clumsy redirection. His news was too important. It was only a matter of time before the third warlord in their host joined the battle. Kishtaar, known as the Howling Silence, had certainly surmised that Sabbreth and Horruskh had left little for her in Skrovenberg and Port Vladovar and had led her forces toward an unspoiled prize. "Can she take that city alone?"
Horruskh shook his head. "Unlikely. She will begin the attack and expect us to support her."
Alliances and rivalries between the three of them were ever-shifting, and the enmity between Sabbreth and Horruskh abruptly burned less bright as they faced a complication that affected them equally.
"So we must," Sabbreth said.
"Then, we march north," Horruskh said, and offered her another of his deformed half-smiles. "A pity you must forgo vengeance on the battle wizard who humbled you."

name: Name
body: Sabbreth was unfazed by Horruskh’s attempt to shame her. While she lay unconscious, the Fellgoeth had shown her many things, but one was seared into her mind. She had seen Borisyuk holding a great silver sword, blood streaming from his eyes, and the heavens aflame above him. She had done far worse to Kapitan Ilari Borisyuk than kill him. She had guided his hand in a killing stroke that would damn him forever.
